title: Trump: Republican lawmakers take Fourth of July trip to Moscow
description_short: Trump: Republican lawmakers take Fourth of July trip to Moscow
description_medium: On July 4, 2018, eight Republican lawmakers met Russian officials in Moscow. Before leaving, they said they would press Russia over election interference; in Moscow, they emphasized improving relations and said they had not come to accuse the country. Russian Duma member Vyacheslav Nikonov called the meeting one of the easiest he had had with U.S. lawmakers.
description_long: Eight Republican members of Congress spent Independence Day 2018 in Moscow: Senators Richard Shelby, Steve Daines, John Hoeven, Ron Johnson, John Kennedy, Jerry Moran and John Thune, and Representative Kay Granger. Before the trip, they told U.S. media they intended to confront Russia about election meddling. In Moscow, they described their purpose as improving relations and said they were not there to accuse Russia. Russian Duma member Vyacheslav Nikonov later called the meeting one of the easiest he had experienced with American lawmakers. The lawmakers’ contrasting public descriptions drew attention because they were representing the United States amid scrutiny of Russian interference in the 2016 election. Ron Johnson later led a Senate investigation involving Ukraine and Joe Biden, which attracted separate concerns about possible Russian influence. That investigation came two years after the Moscow meetings and was a distinct episode. The July visit brought members of both chambers into direct contact with Russian officials on a national holiday associated with American independence. Their remarks in Washington and Moscow offered different accounts of the trip’s purpose.

title: Trump: Mike Huckabee among ‘clown car' of Trump's diplomatic appointments
description_short: Trump: Mike Huckabee among ‘clown car' of Trump's diplomatic appointments
description_medium: In December 2024, Donald Trump named several people with limited diplomatic backgrounds to ambassador posts, including former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee for Israel. International-relations scholar Dennis Jett criticized the pace and qualifications of the nominations. He singled out Huckabee’s rejection of the description of the West Bank as occupied, arguing that the position could complicate his work with Israeli and Palestinian leaders. Trump also nominated Charles Kushner, Kimberly Guilfoyle, Herschel Walker, Matt Whitaker and Tom Barrack.
description_long: In late 2024, President-elect Donald Trump announced a rapid succession of ambassador nominees, prompting scrutiny of their diplomatic experience. The selections included Charles Kushner for France, Kimberly Guilfoyle for Greece, Herschel Walker for the Bahamas, Matt Whitaker for NATO and Tom Barrack for Turkey. Former diplomat and international-relations scholar Dennis Jett criticized the pace and qualifications of the appointments, with Mike Huckabee’s nomination for Israel among his sharpest concerns. Huckabee had no diplomatic service background and had denied that the West Bank was under military occupation, a position at odds with the broad international view. Jett argued that this stance could make Huckabee an ineffective interlocutor in Israeli-Palestinian diplomacy. The criticism focused on whether personal loyalty and political alignment were taking precedence over experience in posts that represent U.S. policy abroad. The nominees included Trump’s family connection Charles Kushner and political allies such as Walker and Guilfoyle. At the time, they were nominees rather than confirmed ambassadors. Their proposed assignments put Trump’s selection criteria in public debate, especially for posts tied to NATO, major allies and regional conflicts.

title: Trump: REPORT: IRS nominee Billy Long had debts paid by donors
description_short: Trump: REPORT: IRS nominee Billy Long had debts paid by donors
description_medium: A Lever News investigation reported that donations to Billy Long’s dormant Senate campaign committee paid off a $130,000 personal loan after Donald Trump nominated him to lead the IRS. The committee raised nearly $137,000 in less than three weeks in January 2025, and Long reimbursed himself, according to filings. Some donors had business before the tax agency; Long’s Senate confirmation was still pending.
description_long: After Donald Trump nominated Billy Long to lead the IRS in December 2024, donations to Long’s dormant 2022 Senate campaign committee surged. Lever News reported that federal filings showed Long had lent the campaign $130,000 and later repaid himself from the new contributions. The committee had raised less than $36,000 over the preceding two years, then collected nearly $137,000 in under three weeks in January 2025. Some donors were connected to businesses with significant matters before the IRS, raising questions about potential conflicts as Long awaited Senate confirmation. Long had also criticized the agency and called for its abolition while in Congress. The timing of the contributions and repayment drew scrutiny because Long was awaiting a position overseeing the same tax agency before which some donors had business. The new receipts were nearly four times what the committee had raised over the prior two years. Those financial ties became part of the Senate confirmation debate.

title: Trump Pressures Barr to Announce Biden Criminal Investigation Before Election
description_short: Trump Pressures Barr to Announce Biden Criminal Investigation Before Election
description_medium: In October 2020, Donald Trump publicly urged Attorney General William Barr to announce a criminal investigation or charges against Joe Biden before Election Day. Trump tied the demand to allegations he called “Obamagate” and to the Ukraine inquiry, and also wanted action involving Barack Obama. Barr declined to announce charges. The demand put pressure on the Justice Department to act against Trump’s electoral opponent during the campaign.
description_long: In the weeks before the November 2020 election, Donald Trump repeatedly pressed Attorney General William Barr to announce a criminal investigation or indictment of Joe Biden before voters went to the polls. Trump linked the demand to “Obamagate” surveillance allegations and the Ukraine investigation, and told aides he wanted Biden “locked up.” He also called for action involving former President Barack Obama. The Los Angeles Times reported that Trump urged Barr to act and appoint someone to investigate Biden and his family. Barr did not announce charges before Election Day. The public demand placed Trump’s political opponent at the center of a call for federal prosecutorial action during the campaign. After Barr resisted, Trump attacked him, according to contemporaneous reporting. The episode became part of the dispute over the Justice Department’s independence from presidential political interests and the use of investigations during an election. Trump made the demand while Biden was his opponent in the presidential race.

title: Trump: ALEC and CNP members meet to discuss stealing the 2020 election
description_short: Trump: ALEC and CNP members meet to discuss stealing the 2020 election
description_medium: At ALEC’s annual meeting on August 14, 2019, members of the American Legislative Exchange Council and Council for National Policy discussed a secret “Political Process Working Group” focused on influencing the 2020 election. Its agenda covered election law, campaign finance, ballot access, redistricting, the Electoral College and voter eligibility. Participants included policy and political figures who later met again in December.
description_long: Members of the American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) and the Council for National Policy (CNP) met during ALEC’s August 2019 annual meeting to discuss a “Political Process Working Group.” ALEC chief executive Lisa Nelson arranged the session, whose stated focus was how to influence the 2020 election. The agenda covered election law, campaign finance, ballot integrity, redistricting, the Electoral College and voter eligibility. ALEC Action president Michael Bowman, Arizona state representative Shawnna Bolick and attorney Cleta Mitchell led the discussion. In a separate session at the same meeting, Mitchell was recorded saying participants would be taught how to gerrymander. Other speakers included Heritage Foundation fellow Hans von Spakovsky, election lawyer Thomas Farr, former Georgia representative Lynn Westmoreland and Texas representative Phil King. The group met again in December. These meetings brought conservative policy groups and political figures together to discuss election rules and strategies for influencing them. The agenda ranged from election administration to voter eligibility, subjects that shape how the 2020 contest would be conducted.

title: Trump: J.D. Vance writes intro to Kevin Roberts book Dawn's Early Light
description_short: Trump: J.D. Vance writes intro to Kevin Roberts book Dawn's Early Light
description_medium: In 2024, Senator J.D. Vance wrote the foreword to Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts’s book Dawn’s Early Light. The New Republic described the text as a “violent” call for conservatives to take up arms. Vance praised Roberts’s political vision, including its emphasis on family, industrial policy and confronting corporate power. After leaked copies drew attention to Project 2025, the book’s title and release plans changed.
description_long: Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts asked Senator J.D. Vance to write the foreword to Dawn’s Early Light, and Vance did so in 2024. The New Republic described the foreword as a “violent” call for conservatives to take up arms. Vance praised Roberts’s vision for a renewed conservatism, including its focus on family, support for American industry and willingness to challenge large corporations’ influence over speech, elections and government. He called for an “offensive” conservatism and echoed Roberts’s image of circling the wagons and loading muskets as political conflict intensified. Leaked copies circulated under two title versions: Dawn’s Early Light: Taking Back Washington to Save America and the more combative Burning Down Washington to Save America. As attention to Project 2025 grew, the title and tagline were revised, and publication was delayed until 2025. Vance’s foreword gave public support to Roberts’s political project and its confrontational rhetoric. The title change and delay followed the controversy over the book’s language and its connection to the Heritage Foundation’s policy agenda.

title: Trump Bombs Houthi Targets in Yemen Amid Signal Chat Scandal
description_short: Trump Bombs Houthi Targets in Yemen Amid Signal Chat Scandal
description_medium: On March 15, 2025, the Trump administration launched strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, citing attacks on Red Sea shipping. That week, senior officials discussed the operation in a Signal group chat that inadvertently included The Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg. Reuters reported that the chat concerned strike coordination, while the administration disputed that classified information had been shared. The disclosure drew scrutiny to operational security and oversight.
description_long: The Trump administration began airstrikes against Houthi targets in Yemen on March 15, 2025, describing them as a response to attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. During the same week, senior officials used a Signal group chat to discuss the operation. National Security Adviser Mike Waltz, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Vice President J.D. Vance were among the officials in the conversation. The Atlantic editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg was inadvertently added and saw messages about the strikes before they began. Reuters reported that the chat concerned coordination of the Yemen operation. The administration disputed that classified information had been shared, while the accidental inclusion of a journalist prompted questions about how officials protected sensitive military discussions. The chat’s timing made its security especially consequential: it concerned an active operation rather than a routine policy debate. The episode drew attention to the government’s use of a consumer messaging service for national-security communications and to the controls governing who could access those discussions.

title: Trump: William Barr testifies that there is no evidence of mail-in voting vulnerability
description_short: Trump: William Barr testifies that there is no evidence of mail-in voting vulnerability
description_medium: At a July 28, 2020 House Judiciary Committee hearing, Attorney General William Barr acknowledged he had no evidence that foreign countries could successfully influence U.S. elections by manufacturing counterfeit mail ballots. This followed months of claims by Donald Trump and allies that expanded mail voting was vulnerable to fraud. Barr had repeated the possibility in interviews but offered “common sense,” rather than evidence, when questioned.
description_long: For months before the 2020 election, Donald Trump and Republican allies warned that expanded mail voting during the COVID-19 pandemic could be manipulated, including through counterfeit ballots. Attorney General William Barr repeated those claims in interviews. During a July 28, 2020 House Judiciary Committee hearing, Representative Mary Gay Scanlon asked whether Barr had evidence that foreign countries could sway U.S. elections by manufacturing ballots. Barr said he did not, adding that he had “common sense.” Scanlon noted that absentee voting was used in every state and that several states had long conducted elections primarily by mail; Barr also acknowledged that the military used mail ballots. His testimony exposed a gap between the administration’s public warnings and the evidence Barr could provide for the specific scenario he described. The exchange came as voting procedures were a major issue in the final months of the campaign. Barr was asked specifically about foreign actors manufacturing ballots; his answer did not address every type of election-administration risk.

title: Trump orders creation of specialized National Guard units to crush civil unrest
description_short: Trump orders creation of specialized National Guard units to crush civil unrest
description_medium: On August 25, 2025, Donald Trump directed the Pentagon to organize National Guard members into rapid-reaction units for domestic deployments, including a specialized unit in Washington, D.C. The order described their purpose as supporting law enforcement and maintaining public safety. It also contemplated deputizing D.C. Guard members to enforce federal law, raising questions about military involvement in civilian policing and legal limits.
description_long: Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon on August 25, 2025, to prepare Army and Air National Guard members for short-notice deployments assisting federal, state and local law enforcement during civil disturbances. The administration described the units as a rapid-reaction force intended to ensure public safety. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was directed to establish a specialized unit within the D.C. National Guard for public order in the capital, with members to be deputized to enforce federal law. The order would expand the Guard’s potential role in domestic law enforcement. The Posse Comitatus Act generally limits the use of federal military forces for civilian policing, subject to exceptions. Retired Major General Randy Manner warned that repeatedly using the Guard in domestic law-enforcement roles could normalize militarized policing. The order placed the boundaries between civilian authorities and the military at issue, particularly because it contemplated federal-law enforcement duties for Guard members. It also raised questions about which legal exception, if any, would govern a future deployment under the plan.

title: Trump: DHS: White supremacists & Russian propaganda are the greatest threats to the U.S.
description_short: Trump: DHS: White supremacists & Russian propaganda are the greatest threats to the U.S.
description_medium: On October 6, 2020, the Department of Homeland Security released a completed annual threat assessment identifying white-supremacist violent extremists as the deadliest domestic terrorist threat in recent years and Russia as a leading source of disinformation. The report followed months of disputes over DHS’s handling of those threats. Acting Secretary Chad Wolf said he was particularly concerned about lethal white-supremacist attacks.
description_long: The Department of Homeland Security released its completed annual threat assessment on October 6, 2020. The report identified white-supremacist violent extremists as the deadliest domestic terrorist threat in recent years and described Russia as a leading covert influence actor and source of disinformation in the United States. Acting DHS Secretary Chad Wolf wrote that he was particularly concerned about lethal attacks by white-supremacist extremists. The release followed months of reporting and controversy over whether DHS officials had downplayed intelligence about Russian influence and domestic extremism. Earlier reporting also described delays in completing the assessment and disputes inside the department over how those threats were characterized. The published assessment put both violent white-supremacist activity and foreign disinformation among the threats facing the country. Its release came amid public disagreement over the agency’s handling of those issues and over the information made available to policymakers and the public.
